property_summary: For every input, the reference contract C reports its paused state truthfully via paused() returning the internal _paused flag; the mutant inverts this value so paused() returns the negation and thus violates this property for some inputs.

For any sequence of calls, the public paused() accessor must reflect the internal pause flag (_paused) truthfully (i.e. paused() == false immediately after initialize and before any pause/unpause), but the mutant inverts that return causing paused() to differ for some inputs.

For every input address acting as the caller, the reference contract's paused() view returns the actual internal pause flag (i.e. paused() == false immediately after initialize and before any pause/unpause by that caller), while the mutant inverts the returned value causing paused() to differ for some caller inputs.

For every input, the reference contract's paused() view returns the actual internal _paused flag (i.e. equals c.paused() == (address(c).balance, but more simply: paused() matches the internal flag set by _pause/_unpause); the mutant inverts the returned boolean so for some admissible sequence the returned value differs — we assert that immediately after initialization paused() == false, which the mutant will violate because it returns true.

For any nonzero admin caller and any address input, calling updateLRTConfig on the reference contract never sets lrtConfig to the zero address (it reverts if given zero); the mutant removed the check and thus allows lrtConfig to become the zero address for that input.

For any caller that has the LRT admin role, calling updateLRTConfig with any address must never leave lrtConfig equal to address(0) on the correct contract (it reverts when passed zero); the mutant removing the non-zero check allows lrtConfig to become zero for input address(0), violating this invariant.

For any admin caller and any input address, calling updateLRTConfig never succeeds in setting lrtConfig to address(0) on the correct contract (it either reverts or leaves a non-zero lrtConfig); the mutant (which removes the non-zero-address check) allows a successful call that sets lrtConfig to address(0).

For any caller that is the LRT admin, calling updateLRTConfig(addr) on the correct contract never results in lrtConfig() returning address(0) (the call reverts if addr == address(0)); the mutant that removes the non-zero-address check allows a successful call that sets lrtConfig() to address(0).

For any caller that is the LRT admin, calling updateLRTConfig(addr) either reverts or results in lrtConfig() != address(0) on the correct contract; the mutant (which removed the non-zero-address check) can succeed and set lrtConfig() == address(0) for addr == address(0).

After calling updateLRTConfig(newAddr) the contract emits UpdatedLRTConfig with the new address (and thus the stored lrtConfig getter equals the emitted address); the mutant emits the previous address instead, so emitting the updated address no longer holds for some input.

For any nonzero new lrtConfig address and a caller with LRT admin role, calling updateLRTConfig(newAddr) results in the emitted UpdatedLRTConfig event carrying the new address (the stored lrtConfig equals the emitted address); the mutant emits the previous address instead and so will violate this rule for some inputs.

For any nonzero new lrtConfig address provided by an LRT admin, after calling updateLRTConfig(newAddr) the UpdatedLRTConfig event's single indexed address equals the new lrtConfig address (i.e. the stored lrtConfig getter equals the emitted event value); the mutant emits the previous address instead and therefore violates this rule for some inputs.

For any nonzero new lrtConfig address and an LRT admin caller, calling updateLRTConfig(newAddr) sets the stored lrtConfig to newAddr (the getter returns newAddr); the mutant still sets the stored value but emits the previous address in the event, which can be detected by observing that the stored getter equals the just-set parameter while the mutant's emitted value would differ for some inputs.

For any nonzero lrtConfigAddr and caller with LRT admin role, calling updateLRTConfig(lrtConfigAddr) emits UpdatedLRTConfig carrying the new address (equal to the updated getter); the mutant emits the previous address instead, so the emitted address != getter for some inputs.

For any caller address, the reference contract allows updateLRTConfig to be called iff the caller has DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE; the mutant inverts that check so non-admins can call it and admins are rejected, violating this rule for some callers.

For any caller address, the correct contract allows updateLRTConfig(...) to succeed iff the caller holds the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE in lrtConfig; the mutant inverts this check and will reject admin callers (or allow non-admins), so there exist caller addresses for which behavior differs.

For any caller address, the reference contract allows updateLRTConfig(...) to succeed iff the caller has the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE in the configured lrtConfig; the mutant inverts that check causing calls by an admin to be rejected (or non-admins accepted), so there exist caller addresses for which updateLRTConfig succeeds on the reference but fails on the mutant.

For any caller address that is granted DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE in the configured lrtConfig, calling updateLRTConfig(...) should succeed on the reference contract; the mutant inverts the role check and will reject such admin callers (making the call fail for some admin addresses).

For any caller address, the reference allows updateLRTConfig(...) to succeed iff the caller is granted DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE in the configured lrtConfig; the mutant inverts the check and will reject such admin callers (or allow non-admins), so there exist callers for which the mutant's success differs from the reference.

For any non-zero lrtConfigAddr, after initialize(lrtConfigAddr) completes, the reference sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10, whereas the mutant sets it to 0 (so the invariant maxNodeDelegatorCount == 10 holds for the reference for all inputs but is violated by the mutant for some input).

After calling initialize(lrtConfigAddr) with any non-zero address, the reference contract always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10; the mutant sets it to 0 for some inputs, so asserting that c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() == 10 distinguishes them.

For any non-zero lrtConfigAddr passed to initialize, the correct contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to a strictly positive value (>=1), whereas the mutant initializes it to 0; therefore after initialize(...) the reference always reports maxNodeDelegatorCount > 0 but the mutant can report 0.

After calling initialize(lrtConfigAddr) with any non-zero lrtConfigAddr, the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to a value equal to the length limit it enforces when adding node delegators: i.e., adding exactly maxNodeDelegatorCount new node delegators to an initially-empty queue succeeds, while the mutant (with maxNodeDelegatorCount = 0) will revert when attempting to add any non-zero-length list; the property asserts that initialize then immediately allows adding a non-empty list of length N when N <= reported maxNodeDelegatorCount.

After calling initialize(lrtConfigAddr) with any non-zero address, the reference C allows a call to addNodeDelegatorContractToQueue with length == reported maxNodeDelegatorCount (i.e., adding up to the returned maxNodeDelegatorCount entries succeeds), while the mutant that sets maxNodeDelegatorCount = 0 will reject adding any non-zero-length list; the property asserts that calling addNodeDelegatorContractToQueue with length equal to c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() succeeds (does not revert).

For any non-zero lrtConfig address input, the correct contract always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to the constant 10 after initialize(...) returns; the mutant instead sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to the numeric value of the provided address, thereby differing for many inputs.

After initialize(lrtConfigAddr) returns, the correct contract always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount == 10 for any non-zero lrtConfigAddr, whereas the mutant sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to uint256(uint160(lrtConfigAddr)) and thus differs for many addresses.

For any non-zero lrtConfigAddr the reference C always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 after initialize(lrtConfigAddr) returns; the mutant instead sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to uint256(uint160(lrtConfigAddr)) and thus will differ for many addresses.

For any non-zero lrtConfigAddr the reference sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 after initialize(...) returns; the mutant sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to uint256(uint160(lrtConfigAddr)) which differs for many addresses, so there exists an address input making the stored maxNodeDelegatorCount != 10.

For every nonzero lrtConfigAddr input the correct contract's initialize(...) always leaves maxNodeDelegatorCount equal to 10; the mutant violates this for any lrtConfigAddr whose uint256(uint160(addr)) != 10 (so there exist fuzzed addresses that make the mutant store a different value).
